title: Why SC's plan to end backlog failed
primary_topics: Why the SC's July 31, 2007 'Internal Policy to Achieve and Maintain a Zero Backlog' (A.M. No. 06-2-10-SC) failed
Empirical worsening: backlog from 8,741 cases (Jan 31, 2007) to 14,491 cases (Dec 31, 2016) per Gio-Samar v. DOTC (March 12, 2019)
The plan's content: 1,000 signed decisions/year cap, minute-resolution disposition of routine petitions, monitoring chain
Why the plan failed in implementation: secrecy ('not for release'), successors inheriting backlog without awareness, non-uniform compliance
Prescription: make the resolution public and publish per-justice caseloads for transparency
sub_topics: A.M. No. 06-2-10-SC dated July 31, 2007 -- drafted by Justice Antonio T. Carpio; approved by Court
Plan premise: Court can promulgate average 1,000 signed decisions/year; accepting >1,000 creates yearly backlog
Rule: cases accepted for signed decisions should not exceed 1,000/year; the rest dismissed by minute resolutions
Total caseload Jan 31, 2007: 8,741; projected end-of-year backlog: 3,201
To clear 3,201 backlog: accept only 500 signed-decision cases in next 6.5 years (102 En Banc + 166 per Division, with note that 166 should be 133 to keep total ≤500)
Monitoring chain: clerk of court (En Banc), three deputy clerks (Divisions), judicial staff heads (per justice)
Maintenance rule: keep 1,000 signed decisions/year until backlog cleared; thereafter accept 500-1,000/year, with accepted cases ≤ promulgated cases for the year

Minute-resolution criteria: cases that (1) don't involve novel questions of law, (2) merely reiterate settled doctrines, (3) in substance raise questions of fact, (4) don't show grave abuse of discretion
Plan was 'internal resolution -- not for release'; CJ obtained copy only 'two weeks ago'
Gio-Samar vs DOTC (March 12, 2019) -- Court's unanimous admission of 14,491 cases at end of 2016
Apparent compliance: 'some incumbents like Justices Carpio, Diosdado M. Peralta, Mariano C. Del Castillo and Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe faithfully followed the plan and have no backlog'

Cause of failure: Court took in more signed-decision cases than acceptable; retiring justices left backlog to successors who probably didn't know about the plan because it was promulgated 'not for release' in 2007 before their appointments
Prescription: publish A.M. No. 06-2-10-SC and per-justice caseloads; make caseload monitoring transparent
signature_phrases: average of 1,000 signed decisions per year
All other cases reaching the Court should be dismissed through minute resolutions
the plan was not implemented properly
merely left the backlog to their successors

laws_treaties: A.M. No. 06-2-10-SC (PH SC administrative resolution, July 31, 2007) -- Internal Policy to Achieve and Maintain a Zero Backlog
events: Jan 31, 2007 -- caseload baseline of 8,741 documented in plan footnote 2
March 12, 2019 -- Gio-Samar vs DOTC unanimously admits worsened backlog
~April 2019 -- CJ obtains plan copy 'two weeks ago'

stances.claim: The SC's July 31, 2007 plan (A.M. No. 06-2-10-SC) drafted by Justice Carpio was 'viable and workable' in design -- it set a hard 1,000-signed-decisions/year output ceiling, capped acceptance at that level (500 over 6.5 years to absorb the existing 3,201 backlog), specified minute-resolution criteria for routine cases, and built a three-tier monitoring chain (clerk, deputy clerks, judicial staff heads).
stances.rhetorical_move: design-defense (the plan itself was not the problem)

stances.claim: The plan nonetheless failed empirically -- backlog grew from 8,741 (Jan 31, 2007) to 14,491 (Dec 31, 2016) per the Court's own unanimous admission in Gio-Samar vs DOTC (March 12, 2019) -- because it was not implemented properly: the Court took in more signed-decision cases than the cap, cases were not disposed by signed decisions and minute resolutions per the plan's detailed protocol, and retiring justices 'merely left the backlog to their successors who probably did not even know about the plan,' which had been promulgated 'not for release' in 2007 before many incumbents joined.
stances.rhetorical_move: implementation-failure diagnosis with specific causal channels

stances.claim: Compliance was not uniform: 'some incumbents like Justices Carpio, Diosdado M. Peralta, Mariano C. Del Castillo and Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe faithfully followed the plan and have no backlog, even if the Court itself carries a hefty caseload' -- demonstrating that individual-justice compliance is feasible within institutional non-compliance.
stances.rhetorical_move: named-compliance evidence (compliance is possible; the failure is collective)

stances.claim: The corrective prescription is transparency: 'with due respect,' the resolution should be made public 'instead of being kept in the Court's labyrinths' so new justices learn of the plan and can follow it diligently, and per-justice caseloads should be published to enable closer monitoring.
stances.confidence: prescriptive with deference marker ('with due respect')

notable_anecdotes: CJ's own disclosure: 'I did not know this plan until two weeks ago, when I got a copy of A.M. No. 06-2-10-SC' -- a former Chief Justice acknowledging he discovered an SC internal-policy resolution belatedly, the empirical proof of its 'not for release' opacity problem.

The plan's footnote-2 baseline -- 'The total caseload of the Court as of 31 January 2007 (was) 8,741. It estimated that at the end of that year, the backlog (would) be 3,201 cases' -- surfaced verbatim, making the document feel auditable.

The mathematical inconsistency CJ flags in brackets -- '166 [should be 133 only, otherwise the total would exceed 500] per Division, per year' -- a former CJ catching an arithmetic slip in the plan's text without softening it.

The contrast between the Court's collective failure (8,741 → 14,491) and the named-compliance group (Carpio, Peralta, Del Castillo, Perlas-Bernabe with 'no backlog') -- establishing that compliance is structurally feasible, not aspirational.
The 'labyrinths' image for SC internal opacity -- 'instead of being kept in the Court's labyrinths' -- physicalizing institutional secrecy as architecture.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines why the Supreme Court's July 31, 2007 'Internal Policy to Achieve and Maintain a Zero Backlog' (A.M. No. 06-2-10-SC), drafted by Justice Antonio T. Carpio, failed empirically -- even though the Court itself unanimously admitted in Gio-Samar vs DOTC (March 12, 2019) that its docket had grown from 8,741 cases (January 31, 2007 baseline in the plan's footnote 2) to '14,491 cases in its docket' as of December 31, 2016. He summarizes the plan's design: the Court can promulgate an average of 1,000 signed decisions per year, so accepting more than 1,000 yearly creates structural backlog; routine cases (those not involving novel questions of law, merely reiterating settled doctrines, raising questions of fact in substance, or not showing grave abuse of discretion) must be dismissed by minute resolutions; for 6.5 years, signed-decision acceptances should be capped at 500 total (102 En Banc plus 166 per Division -- CJ notes in brackets that 166 should be 133 to keep the total under 500); and a three-tier monitoring chain (clerk of court, three deputy clerks, judicial staff heads of each justice) tracks acceptances. He discloses he 'did not know this plan until two weeks ago' because it was promulgated 'not for release.' In his 'humble opinion' the plan was 'viable and workable,' but it 'was not implemented properly': the Court accepted more cases than the cap, cases were not disposed in the manner the plan specified, and 'some retiring justices merely left the backlog to their successors who probably did not even know about the plan, considering that it was promulgated not for release in 2007 prior to their assumption of office.' Yet some incumbents -- Justices Carpio, Diosdado M. Peralta, Mariano C. Del Castillo, and Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe -- 'faithfully followed the plan and have no backlog, even if the Court itself carries a hefty caseload,' establishing that compliance is structurally feasible. 'With due respect,' CJ urges the Court to make the resolution public 'instead of being kept in the Court's labyrinths' so new justices can learn and follow it, and to publish per-justice caseloads for closer monitoring.
